Dynamic Workflows vs Skills vs Subagents: What are the differences?
Anthropic just dropped a new orchestration feature called
Dynamic Workflows
which can spawn hundreds of subagents to take on massive tasks.
It lets Claude write a script that fires off subagents, runs them in parallel, and hands you back one checked result.
But how exactly does it work, and how does it differ from the other agentic development approaches using subagents and skills?
According to the internal team at Anthropic, they built this feature a couple months ago, and it has slowly become their daily driver.

What is a Dynamic Workflow?

This feature lets Claude write a script that fires off subagents, runs them in parallel, and hands you back one checked result.

New in Claude Code (research preview): dynamic workflows. Claude writes an orchestration script on the fly, then spins up a large fleet of coordinated subagents in parallel to take on your most complex tasks. Use the word "workflow" in a prompt to get started.
It was released alongside the Claude Opus 4.8 which is more capable: SWE-bench Pro (from 64.3 to 69.2) and noticeably more honest about its own work.
Type “workflow” into a prompt and Claude writes an orchestration plan, then follows it to the letter.
That strict plan is the point. Every stage runs in the right order, even across hundreds of agents.
One run can fan out wide, but not infinitely. Anthropic caps it at 16 agents running at once and 1,000 total per workflow.
Note: Dynamic Workflows are in research preview. They run in the Claude Code CLI, Desktop, and VS Code extension, plus the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry. They’re on by default for Max, Team, and API users. On Enterprise, an admin turns them on first.
You also need Claude Code v2.1.154 or later to see the feature at all.

Subagents vs Skill vs Dynamic Workflows

Subagents and skills both shipped in earlier Claude Code updates. So what does a workflow add?
It comes down to who holds the plan.
A subagent leaves Claude in charge. It decides which worker to spawn next, turn by turn. The problem is context. Every result an agent returns lands back in Claude’s context window and eats your tokens.
A skill hands Claude a list of steps written in a Markdown file. The steps are reusable, but Claude still runs the flow inside the conversation.
A workflow moves the plan into code. A JavaScript script decides what to launch, in what order, with whatever loops or conditions the job needs.
The state lives in script variables, not the conversation. Only the final answer comes back to you.
Subagents, skills, and workflows all help Claude break work into smaller parts, but they do not operate at the same level.
  • Subagents: When Claude needs extra hands.
  • Skills: When Claude needs reusable instructions.
  • Workflows: When the plan itself belongs in code.
Here is the simple rule:
Use a subagent or a skill when the plan fits in a few steps Claude can hold in context. Use a workflow when the plan is repeatable, stateful, and too big for
that.How
to Use Dynamic Workflows

How to Use Dynamic Workflows

Since Workflows is the newest development approach among the three, let me show you an example of how it works.
First, switch your model to Opus 4.8. Type /model and pick it from the list.
There are two ways to start a workflow.
The first is explicit. Put “workflow” in your prompt and Claude Code highlights it, then writes a one-off JavaScript script for that task instead of working turn by turn.
Prompt: Create a workflow that audits this project for bugs and security issues, checks the codebase for broken logic, unsafe API routes, weak authentication, missing authorization, exposed secrets, dependency risks, and possible data leaks, then produces a clear Markdown report with severity levels, affected file paths, short explanations, and recommended fixes.
Once it’s generated, Claude Code shows you the planned phases before it runs anything.
While it’s running, type /workflows to track progress.
In my run, six agents audited the project in parallel. The view refreshes constantly, so each agent’s status updates in real time.
When the run finishes, every agent flips to “completed,” with its prompt, activity, and outcome attached.
The whole-project security audit took 4 minutes and 41 seconds.
Token warning: A workflow can burn far more tokens than a normal Claude Code session, because every agent carries its own context overhead. Anthropic recommends starting on a small, scoped task to learn the cost before you point it at a full repo or a migration across thousands of files.
In this example, the audit consumed 1.1 million tokens.
Press s to save the report or escape to discard it.

The second way is automatic, and it’s called ultracode.
Turn it on with /effort ultracode. It pairs xhigh reasoning with automatic workflow orchestration.
Open the effort slider and you’ll see a small animation when ultracode is selected.
With ultracode on, Claude decides for itself whether a task needs a workflow.
One request can turn into several workflows in sequence: one to understand the code, one to make the change, one to verify it.

Real-world use cases

Anthropic’s blog shares two enterprise testimonials.
Alessio Vallero, Senior Engineering Manager at Klarna, has used workflows for discovery and review across large codebases. His team found dead code and cleanup that static analysis kept missing.
Ken Takao, Lead Systems Engineer at CyberAgent, says workflows fill the gap between firing off one subagent and building a full agent team. That lets his team trust longer runs without losing visibility.
Three patterns keep showing up.
  • Repo-wide bug hunting. Claude runs parallel searches across files and folders, then a separate pass verifies each finding and drops the false positives.
  • Large-scale migrations. Framework swaps, API deprecations, and language ports across thousands of files. The Bun rewrite (Zig to Rust, 750,000 lines, eleven days) is the most extreme public example so far.
  • Critical verification with adversarial agents. When a wrong answer is expensive, the workflow makes independent attempts, has them attack each other’s results, and only delivers the conclusions that survive.

Availability of Dynamic Workflows

It is in research preview as of May 28, 2026, across the Claude Code CLI, Desktop, and VS Code extension, plus the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry.
They’re on by default for Max, Team, and API users. On Enterprise they stay off until an admin enables them, so companies can control the higher token bills.
